k-accomplished.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> climbs a <radical>road</radical>, its surface <radical>split</radical> into ruts of packed <radical>earth</radical>. The flock keeps stalling, but the last one clears the rise: the job is <kanji>accomplished</kanji>.
k-accomplished.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

k-ancestor.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>altar</radical> stands on the left. Beside it, an <radical>eye</radical> lies flat above a line of <radical>ground</radical> — a portrait propped over the offerings. Somebody long dead looks back at you off that shelf: your <kanji>ancestor</kanji>.
k-ancestor.reading_mnemonic: So is the small catch of sound the incense makes when it takes light at the altar — 「<reading>そ</reading>」 — and for a second the eye in the portrait seems to move. One syllable, once a year, for the ancestor. そ.

k-breath.meaning_mnemonic: Your own <radical>self</radical> sits on top — the nose you point at when you mean you — with your <radical>heart</radical> underneath. Nose above, heart below, and running between them all day is the one thing you never decide to do: <kanji>breath</kanji>.
k-breath.reading_mnemonic: Soku is the swimmer who comes up after far too long under and takes one enormous ragged gulp — 「<reading>そく</reading>」 — nose first, heart going like a hammer. That is what a breath you badly needed sounds like. そく.

k-daughter.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> stands at the left, beside the shape of <radical>stopping</radical>: an eye that has seen something, a foot that will not move. She is planted in the doorway, arms folded — not going out tonight. Somebody's <kanji>daughter</kanji>.
k-daughter.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」. It is the address for a girl of good family who is not allowed out tonight. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

k-daytime.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> lies flat under a <radical>drop</radical> of sweat, the <radical>sun</radical> pinned beneath it against a line of <radical>ground</radical>. No shade is left; work has stopped: the flattening middle of <kanji>daytime</kanji>.
k-daytime.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the loyal mouse will not nap through it. While every other body is flat out he stands at his post in the full sun, squeaking 「<reading>ちゅう</reading>」 on the hour so that nobody oversleeps. Absurdly devoted, ちゅう, right through the worst of it.

k-doctor.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>box on its side</radical>, its open mouth turned towards you, an <radical>arrow</radical> lying inside — the one they just drew out of you. The lid comes down over the arrowhead and the wound both. Whoever owns that box is the <kanji>doctor</kanji>.
k-doctor.reading_mnemonic: Ii is the noise she makes while examining you: one short noncommittal 「<reading>い</reading>」 as she looks at the wound, and another as she drops the arrow into the tray. Nothing whatsoever about い tells you whether it is bad news.

k-end.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up, branches <radical>split</radical> aside. A <radical>lid</radical> stroke lies atop, longer than the <radical>one</radical> below — the twig's last inch: the <kanji>end</kanji>.
k-end.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

k-evening.meaning_mnemonic: Three strokes and nothing else: a curve like the shoulder of a hill, with one line falling through it. It is the moon, half up, caught the moment the light goes flat and blue, the hush of <radical>evening</radical> settling in. The whole character is one picture of <kanji>evening</kanji> starting.
k-evening.reading_mnemonic: Seki comes out onto his step at this hour every night, and you hear him before you see him — that wet, rattling 「<reading>せき</reading>」 of a cough carrying right down the street. When せき starts up, the light has gone.

k-father.meaning_mnemonic: Two arms cross at the top, two legs brace wide underneath — the stance of a <radical>father</radical> planted in the doorway, arms folded, filling the frame. He is waiting to hear what you have to say. Everybody recognises that silhouette: <kanji>father</kanji>.
k-father.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the long breath out through the nose that he gives you instead of an answer — 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 — arms still folded. Not angry. Not pleased either. Just ふ, and you will be hearing it for the rest of your life.

k-friend.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, met by a <radical>right hand</radical> rising underneath. Two hands close on each other, nobody paid, nobody in charge: that is a <kanji>friend</kanji>.
k-friend.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is always there before you, hand already out. He draws the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

k-gone.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> sits on top, underneath a sealed <radical>cocoon</radical> tucked out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped up and went under the soil. Dig the mound over: nothing is left. It is <kanji>gone</kanji>.
k-gone.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

k-he.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, beside a hide hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it and is already down the road. That man you point at and cannot name: <kanji>he</kanji>.
k-he.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」. By the time you finish it, he is round the corner. Every time you catch sight of him: ひ.

k-heart.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, shoved to the back with <radical>rice</radical> and something <radical>big</radical> on top. You walk through every room to reach it; nobody outside the family does. The deepest room is the <kanji>heart</kanji>.
k-heart.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

k-husband.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>big</radical> figure — the <radical>person</radical> with arms flung wide. Lay one bar on top like a <radical>lid</radical>, so <radical>two</radical> strokes sit there, not one: his topknot pin. Grown and married: <kanji>husband</kanji>.
k-husband.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the same breath out through the nose you learned from his father, inherited exactly — arms folded in the doorway, one 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, no further comment offered. Getting married did not change it in the slightest.

k-me.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the far left, beside him a <radical>big</radical> load: a <radical>sheep</radical> he must carry in. He <radical>splits</radical> it for everyone else before he eats — the humble word he uses for <kanji>me</kanji>.
k-me.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.

k-mister.meaning_mnemonic: Someone sweeps the yard with a <radical>broom</radical>, one <radical>slide</radical> of a stroke clearing the <radical>ground</radical>. He opens his <radical>mouth</radical> with tomorrow's orders: not the emperor, just the man above you, <kanji>mister</kanji>.
k-mister.reading_mnemonic: Kun is the teacher who refuses to use first names. Every boy in the class gets the same syllable barked after his surname — 「<reading>くん</reading>」 — as the seating chart comes out. Tanaka-くん. Sato-くん. It is how you know he means you.

k-morning.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is caught low in a <radical>cross</radical>-braced frame on the left, still climbing, while the <radical>moon</radical> on the right has not gone down. Both are up at once, for twenty minutes a day: <kanji>morning</kanji>.
k-morning.reading_mnemonic: Chou is the long-distance runner who is out before anybody else, and she stretches her greeting the whole length of the street as she passes your window — a long, unreasonably cheerful 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」. If you hear ちょう, the moon is still up.

k-mother.meaning_mnemonic: A figure kneels like a <radical>mother</radical>, arms wrapped round in front of her, two dots marking the breasts that fed you. The entire character is built around those two points — take them out and it becomes a different word. They are the reason you call her <kanji>mother</kanji>.
k-mother.reading_mnemonic: Bo is the one syllable a baby manages long before it manages anything else — 「<reading>ぼ</reading>」 — blown out with a bubble of spit and aimed straight at whoever is holding it. She answers to ぼ years before she answers to her own name.

k-night.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips under as the last <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once the lid is on, nothing more gets in: no sun, no colour. The lid down over the evening: <kanji>night</kanji>.
k-night.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

k-nightfall.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has been let off: the shape on the right squeezes from under the heavy lid, walking off <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done; it drops below the roofline unbid. The sun excused from duty: <kanji>nightfall</kanji>.
k-nightfall.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

k-on-foot.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it a <radical>run</radical> — thigh forward, foot planting, ground loose behind. No horse, no cart, no road worth the name. Whatever gets done today gets done <kanji>on foot</kanji>.
k-on-foot.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle has never once taken a ride. He carries the sample doors on his shell and walks the entire round, and he announces himself at every house with the same syllable before he knocks — 「<reading>と</reading>」. と, and another mile.

k-private.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans on the left, tucked behind it a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the crop in the open, then kept one seed back for yourself: <kanji>private</kanji>.
k-private.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

k-second-1.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> on the left, beside it the <radical>small</radical> mark — one bristle off the very top, thinnest thing on the plant. Slice an hour the same way and the sliver left in your hand is one <kanji>second</kanji>.
k-second-1.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

k-submit.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left; on the right <radical>two</radical> bars over <radical>ground</radical>, each on a <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>split</radical> into legs at the foot. A tray, lifted with both hands for somebody above to take: to <kanji>submit</kanji> a thing.
k-submit.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

k-uncle.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, a <radical>right hand</radical> scooping both up. He is the younger brother: not head of the family, so he gets the small share. Your <kanji>uncle</kanji>.
k-uncle.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

k-what.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the left with a line in hand — a <radical>barb</radical> at its end, a bar of <radical>ground</radical> above the open <radical>mouth</radical>. He hauls something up, stares, mouth open, no idea <kanji>what</kanji> it is.
k-what.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow drops onto the power line above him and looks at the thing on the hook. She has never seen one either. All she manages is one puzzled croak — 「<reading>か</reading>?」 — with a little puff of flame behind it. か? か? Neither of them knows.

k-who.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have talked for ten minutes and the bird still cannot tell which person you mean. It asks the only question left: <kanji>who</kanji>?
k-who.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

k-wife.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, above her a <radical>broom</radical> on its <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>ground</radical> ruled across top. Not sweeping somebody's house — the broom, floor, roof are hers: the <kanji>wife</kanji> running them.
k-wife.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

k-yesterday.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, a <radical>stick</radical> upright on the right with one <radical>slide</radical> of a stroke off it. That stick is a sundial, its shadow scratched beside. The sun moved on; the mark left behind is <kanji>yesterday</kanji>.
k-yesterday.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

k-zero.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> across the top, under a <radical>person</radical> kneeling on bare <radical>ground</radical> as the clerk presses her <radical>stamp</radical> on the ledger. It lands where the crop should count, printing a round <kanji>zero</kanji>.
k-zero.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

k-employee.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a badge shaped like an open <radical>mouth</radical>, clipped above a fat coin-purse of <radical>money</radical>, swinging on a lanyard. At the mountain trail's summit, a gatekeeper won't sell a drink until that badge is stamped and your name goes into the ledger: you're now an <kanji>employee</kanji> of the mountain.
k-employee.reading_mnemonic: The gatekeeper is a retired innkeeper everyone calls <reading>Inn</reading>. She grunts <reading>いん</reading> every time she stamps a badge — one grunt per hire. By dusk, her voice is gone from saying it all day.
k-employee.description: 員 rarely stands alone as a word for 'employee' — it is a suffix meaning roughly 'a person belonging to,' always riding on a job title, company, or club, closer to '-er' than to a stand-alone noun.

k-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: See the whole character as a gear rim cut into jagged points — a grinning mouthful of teeth. At Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cats gnaw the rim like a giant biscuit. Their own teeth file down flat, but the metal only gleams sharper: one hard <radical>tooth</radical> makes the gear a <kanji>cog</kanji>.
k-tooth.reading_mnemonic: One shrine cat, nicknamed <reading>Shii</reading> for the hiss she makes mid-gnaw, clamps onto the bell rim and hisses <reading>し</reading> through the gap where a tooth used to be.

k-body.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a lean <radical>person</radical> outline, with <radical>one</radical> rigid <radical>tree</radical> trunk running straight down its spine, arms locked out to the sides. At Sei's school, the club drags out this same stiff training dummy for every first-aid drill: everyone just calls it the <kanji>body</kanji>.
k-body.reading_mnemonic: Someone always loops a spare <reading>tie</reading> around the training dummy's neck before drills, and the coach barks <reading>たい</reading> to snap the team to attention — same dummy, same crooked tie, every single practice.

k-thing.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a lumpy, unlabeled shape — <radical>not</radical> quite a box, not quite a creature, just a mass with no clean outline. Koichi's lost-and-found bin behind the konbini is just like this: a toy <radical>cow</radical>, a bent umbrella, half a slipper. After six months he labels the whole bin '<kanji>thing</kanji>.'
k-thing.reading_mnemonic: Koichi holds up a single lost <reading>boot</reading> from the bin and grunts <reading>ぶつ</reading> — the general word for 'thing,' because after six unclaimed months, calling it a boot feels oddly specific.

k-meal.meaning_mnemonic: See the whole character as a plate laid out to <radical>eat</radical> from: a heaping bowl of rice on the left, resting on a <radical>cliff</radical>-ledge. Crammed against it is a second helping some <radical>right hand</radical> snuck onto the tray before anyone could stop it. Two portions in one shape: the whole <kanji>meal</kanji>, seconds included.
k-meal.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, slices your whole dinner clean down the center before you can protest — that's just how he works here. You call out his name, <reading>Han</reading>, and he answers with a proud <reading>はん</reading>, holding up two identical plates like it settles the matter.

k-tea.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a steaming cup: delicate <radical>grass</radical> leaves curling up top like visible steam, a little <radical>person</radical> warming his hands round a <radical>tree</radical>-carved cup below. That curling steam over the cup is the whole picture: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
k-tea.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm. He counts the beat out loud — 「<reading>ちゃ</reading>」-cha-cha — until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

k-hit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a dart thrown with quiet <radical>esteem</radical> for its own aim, flight feathers up top, and a <radical>broom</radical>-shaped tail sweeping it dead center into the target below. One clean throw, no wobble: a direct <kanji>hit</kanji>.
k-hit.reading_mnemonic: The dart thrower celebrates his bullseye by kicking the target stand in triumph and instantly regrets it, hopping and hissing through his teeth: <reading>とう</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>! Somehow he still lands the next throw dead center.

k-ill.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a <radical>sickness</radical> lean-to: a slanted roof over a <radical>wide box</radical> of a room. Inside it lies a <radical>person</radical> stretched flat, legs sticking out past a blanket too short to cover them. The whole shape is a tiny room built for one thing: someone too <kanji>ill</kanji> to get up.
k-ill.reading_mnemonic: The former beauty-pageant queen lies flat under the sickroom's too-short blanket, moaning into her pillow. This is the least glamorous she has ever looked: 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, she groans, sounding exactly like the first half of <reading>beauty</reading> gone hoarse.

k-section.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 部 as a squat filing cabinet: a <radical>stand</radical> strut over a slot like an open <radical>mouth</radical>, beside a little <radical>village</radical> of drawers. A clerk yanks the wrong drawer, gets buried in someone else's forms, and slams shut the one marked for his own <kanji>section</kanji>.
k-section.reading_mnemonic: A moth called <reading>Bu</reading> gets shut inside that same drawer overnight and beats its wings against the forms, the frantic drumming going <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, until dawn finally opens the drawer and lets it stagger free.

k-pedestal.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 台 as a squat stone pedestal: a <radical>cocoon</radical>-shaped knob on top, over a wide <radical>mouth</radical> of a base bolted to the ground. Workers winch a bronze statue onto it, and the block doesn't budge under the weight: solid, built for holding something up — a <kanji>pedestal</kanji>.
k-pedestal.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, climbs onto that same pedestal to pose like a statue. One stomp cracks the stone with a boom that rattles windows, and he wails <reading>だい</reading>, <reading>だい</reading> as the block crumbles beneath him.

k-courtyard.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 庭 as a private courtyard behind a lean-to <radical>shelter</radical>: raked white gravel, a crooked pine, and one <radical>jewel</radical>-bright stone lantern. A stubborn goat, <radical>stretching</radical> along the low wall, keeps chewing the ivy. Nobody evicts it from the family's own patch of outside: the <kanji>courtyard</kanji>.
k-courtyard.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper, named <reading>Tei</reading>, sprints after the goat squatting in the courtyard, tripping over the raked gravel and yelling <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>てい</reading> with every failed lunge, gravel spraying across the whole swept quiet.

k-turn.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 番 as a ticket dispenser bolted to a wall, its slots ruled like a tiny <radical>rice field</radical>, spitting out numbered slips kept strictly <radical>separate</radical>. Customers file into line by number, nobody out of place: the pure order of your <kanji>turn</kanji>.
k-turn.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a guard named <reading>Ban</reading> slams a wooden stamp onto the counter each time a new number is called. The crack echoes <reading>ばん</reading> through the shop as the line shuffles forward, one turn at a time.

k-empty.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker jams every coin into the lone vending machine, all steel <radical>construction</radical>. The lever clunks, the tray spins over a <radical>hole</radical> where the snack should drop. No can, no snack, just a hollow clang. Every row sits bare: the whole machine as <kanji>empty</kanji> as the sky above.
k-empty.reading_mnemonic: Still stuck at the summit, the hiker slumps against the machine and lets out a long, pigeon-like <reading>coo</reading> up at the empty sky. 「<reading>くう</reading>」, rising and hollow, over and over, until it's the only sound left on the mountain.

k-brush-stroke.meaning_mnemonic: In the school art room, a boy is told to paint just <radical>one</radical> careful stroke inside the blank canvas, an <radical>open box</radical> of a frame. His hand shakes; the brush skids across a <radical>rice field</radical> grid of guide-lines. It loops corner to corner until smeared black. The teacher pins it up anyway: a <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji> made of every stroke that got away.
k-brush-stroke.reading_mnemonic: Back in the art room, the teacher looks at the smeared frame and can only manage a flat, deflated <reading>gah</reading> — <reading>が</reading> — the sound of someone giving up on a critique before it starts. He staples a ribbon to it anyway and calls it finished.

k-reflect.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman sets his lantern, glass <radical>cover</radical> and all, on a flat rock as the <radical>sun</radical> goes down. The still water lets the flame's light <radical>slide</radical> straight back up, and his own face looks oddly <radical>big</radical> staring down at it. He waves; the water waves back late — exactly what it means to <kanji>reflect</kanji>.
k-reflect.reading_mnemonic: Startled by his own doubled face in the water, the fisherman yelps 「<reading>Ay</reading>」 — 「<reading>えい</reading>」. The river throws the sound straight back at him a beat later, flat and unbothered, same as it did with the light.

k-roof.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini springs a leak the night the first typhoon <radical>arrive</radical>s. Rain drums through a hole in the ceiling onto the onigiri shelf. Koichi hauls up a tarp and lashes it down flat and still as a <radical>body</radical>, muttering that a shop without one is just an expensive puddle. The neighborhood now calls the place the <kanji>roof</kanji> instead of its real name.
k-roof.reading_mnemonic: Weeks later, the tarp is still up, now painted with a crude little <reading>oak</reading> tree Koichi drew himself — <reading>おく</reading> — because customers kept asking what was holding the whole roof together. Nobody has the heart to tell him it's just tarp and string.

k-inst.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has quietly become an institution. The mossy steps lead through a turnstile marking the <radical>beginning</radical> of the queue, under the old <radical>roof</radical>. Beyond it lies a <radical>village</radical> of numbered waiting rooms, staffed by a cat in a visor. That towering bureaucratic compound is one big <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
k-inst.reading_mnemonic: At the same window, the visor cat's ink stamp has half-dried, so every ticket comes out a pale <reading>いん</reading>. She grumbles it sounds like <reading>bean</reading> paste smeared thin, and refuses to fetch a new pad before the shrine's afternoon bell.

k-bureau.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till, Koichi partitions off a booth with a <radical>mouth</radical>-sized service window and nails up a sign reading BUREAU. Every <radical>body</radical> in line — parcels, stamps, tax forms — squeezes through, three queues at once. Koichi just nods, because everyone who reaches window three sounds exactly like they're trying to say <reading>choke</reading>.

k-convenience.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a lone <radical>person</radical> finds a portable toilet bolted beside the vending machine, its door numbered with a single <radical>one</radical>. k-building.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school gym floods every spring, so the committee tears a <radical>mouth</radical> of a doorway through to the old mansion's <radical>roof</radical> next door and calls the echoing ballroom the new gym. k-near.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 近 as a signpost arrow, chopped short by an <radical>axe</radical>, that curled back along the <radical>road</radical> to jab at your own boots. k-near.reading_mnemonic: At that vending machine, the hiker's little brother — pure <reading>kin</reading>, tagging along everywhere — presses his face to the glass and chants the machine's name like a drumbeat: <reading>きん</reading>. He is always, always this close.

k-slow.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the very last runner limps down the <radical>road</radical>, each stride <radical>split</radical> in half by a cramped calf. k-slow.reading_mnemonic: The class hamster, <reading>Chi</reading>, is let loose to race him and loses on purpose, wheezing one flat unimpressed <reading>ち</reading> at the finish line — same track, same dragging in dead last.

k-walk.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 歩 as one <radical>small</radical> sandal print, stamped twice — heel, a <radical>slide</radical> to toe, a <radical>stop</radical> before it lifts. At the riverbank, that print walks itself across the stepping-stones, landing dead center all the way to the far bank: <kanji>walk</kanji>.
k-walk.reading_mnemonic: Halfway across, the fisherman watching from the bank lets out one delighted <reading>ho</reading> — <reading>ほ</reading> — every time the print lands without a splash, cheering each dry step home.

k-exertion.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 勉 as a sweatband wrung out mid-cram with sheer <radical>power</radical>, soaking the page underneath. In Koichi's konbini, a student camped by the onigiri shelf pulls an all-nighter, refusing to be <radical>exempt</radical>, wringing the band out again and again: pure <kanji>exertion</kanji>.
k-exertion.reading_mnemonic: The clerk ringing up onigiri all night, <reading>Ben</reading>, groans the same sympathetic <reading>べん</reading> every time the sweatband hits the counter, cheering the cramming on until the beeping till finally goes quiet.

k-paper.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a flat gray sheet dragged from the river current, its <radical>thread</radical>-thin fibers refusing to line up. A woman known only by her <radical>family name</radical> presses it against a wooden frame in the shallows, and by the time the sun dries it stiff, it lies flat, blank, and waiting: <kanji>paper</kanji>.
k-paper.reading_mnemonic: At the same riverbank, a heron picks through the drying pulp and hisses 「<reading>し</reading>」 as the wet sheet slips under its feet. That flat <reading>sheesh</reading> of air escaping is the exact noise you make when you finally get the paper flat.

k-window.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the back wall of Koichi's konbini, once a tight little <radical>cocoon</radical>, windowless — until someone punches a single square <radical>hole</radical> through the plaster at eye level. Light floods in, and every customer's <radical>heart</radical> goes straight to that bright square cut into the dark: a <kanji>window</kanji>.
k-window.reading_mnemonic: At the same konbini, a raccoon dog crashes through the new opening chasing a dropped onigiri and skids across the tile. The clerk can only gasp 「<reading>そう</reading>」 — that flat English <reading>so</reading> of someone watching it happen with no better word for it.

k-true.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the offering box has a slot cut in a <radical>cross</radical>, wide enough to <radical>split</radical> a coin clean in two. A single carved <radical>eye</radical> watches from the lintel above, fixed on <radical>one</radical> coin the whole time it spins. It never blinks and never looks away, the way a shrine cat won't look away from a fish. That unwavering, unblinking watch — nothing hidden, nothing faked — is <kanji>true</kanji>.
k-true.reading_mnemonic: One of the shrine cats leaps for the ladle, misjudges the step, and slams its shin against the stand. It yowls 「<reading>しん</reading>」, the sound of the English word <reading>shin</reading>, before limping off — the truest reaction any cat has given all day.

k-cut.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the gym teacher's whistle at Sei's school, blown so hard the long note doesn't fade — a <radical>sword</radical>-swift stroke slices it off mid-breath, the tail curling away like the bowl of a <radical>spoon</radical>. That dead, clean stop is the whole idea drawn into one character: <kanji>cut</kanji>.
k-cut.reading_mnemonic: A stray dog dashes onto Sei's field mid-drill, and the whistle cuts dead again: 「<reading>せつ</reading>」. That's the clipped English <reading>set</reading> the teacher barks before chasing it off, the severed note still hanging where the sound should continue.

k-wind.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's poncho balloons into one huge sail, hood snapping sideways, a moth trapped inside hunting for an exit that isn't there. The poncho leans hard in one direction, cloth cracking like a whip. That swollen, straining shape is <radical>wind</radical> itself — nothing else moves <kanji>air</kanji> like that.
k-wind.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the trail, the hiker doubles over and breathes out one long 「<reading>ふう</reading>」. It's the same winded <reading>phew</reading> you'd sigh after a gust knocks you sideways, air rushing out just like the air that knocked you there.

k-move.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stacked crate of onigiri suddenly rolls off on a single <radical>stick</radical> axle, one <radical>slide</radical> of momentum carrying it toward the door. Its <radical>power</radical> comes from nowhere obvious — no cord, no battery, just <radical>one</radical> crate deciding to go. That crate, suddenly alive and unstoppable, is <kanji>move</kanji> itself.
k-move.reading_mnemonic: Koichi lurches out of the way and yelps <reading>どう</reading> — a flat, startled <reading>doh</reading> — as the crate rumbles past the beeping till and rocks the onigiri shelf on its way through.

k-cool.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the water freezes over so fast that a dragonfly gets sealed inside the <radical>ice</radical>, wings still spread. Beside it, a <radical>person</radical>'s single bootprint is <radical>stamp</radical>ed into the same frozen crust. The whole surface holds that <radical>one</radical> frozen, glassy chill: <kanji>cool</kanji>.
k-cool.reading_mnemonic: A swimmer named <reading>Ray</reading> wades into the river and the cold hits so fast he gasps <reading>れい</reading> — like shouting his own name — freezing mid-step right where the dragonfly sits trapped in the ice.

k-music.meaning_mnemonic: In the schoolyard, a lone <radical>tree</radical> is strung branch to branch with dozens of tiny <radical>white</radical> bells that ring with an <radical>ice</radical>-sharp chime. A squirrel scrambling up sets off a cascade of ringing that spreads through the hallways, so rich that class doesn't mind the interruption: that whole chiming tree is <kanji>music</kanji>.
k-music.reading_mnemonic: Sei gawks up at the tree, mouth open, murmuring <reading>がく</reading> — pure <reading>gawk</reading> — unable to look away from the bells still swinging long after the squirrel is gone.

k-transmit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 伝 as a hunched <radical>person</radical>, a courier crouched on Grandma Kane's steps, passing a paper folded tight as a <radical>cocoon</radical> from <radical>two</radical> hands to the next. Cats bat it along underfoot until it lands under the enormous bell. The message has crossed the shrine untouched: <kanji>transmit</kanji>.
k-transmit.reading_mnemonic: At the bell, an eel called <reading>Denny</reading> lives coiled in the rope. Anyone who tugs the bell to ring it gets a jolt, yelping <reading>でん</reading> as the shock jumps up their arm. The courier's paper still gets through — Denny just likes his cut of the news.

k-question.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 問 as a <radical>gate</radical> with a <radical>mouth</radical> built into the crossbar, shouting through the bars at Sei's school. A latecomer rattles the locked gate, and the mouth shouts back, demanding to know why they're late. Nobody gets in without answering the gate's <kanji>question</kanji>.
k-question.reading_mnemonic: Outside that same gate, Mon-Bun — the scholarly rabbit twins — bicker without pause, blaming each other for muddling the question. They let out one long identical <reading>moan</reading> that comes out as <reading>もん</reading>, echoing off the bars, and they're still moaning it when the gate creaks open.

k-trip.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 旅 as a tattered <radical>chevron</radical> flag flapping at the head of the trail, pointing the <radical>direction</radical> for a whole line of hikers trudging after it. Nobody questions where it leads; they just follow, boots slipping on gravel, until the trail spits them out at the vending machine on top. That staggering line is a <kanji>trip</kanji>.
k-trip.reading_mnemonic: Leading them is a llama guide named <reading>Rio</reading>, bleating <reading>りょ</reading> at every switchback to keep the line moving. By the vending machine he collapses first, legs folded, still muttering it between breaths.

k-attend.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 仕 as a <radical>person</radical>, a clerk standing bolt upright behind Koichi's till, spine straight as a blade, saluting every customer like a <radical>samurai</radical> posted at his station. He never sits, never slouches, just attends the register from open to close. That rigid stance is the whole meaning: <kanji>attend</kanji>.
k-attend.reading_mnemonic: Beside him works a hedgehog cashier named <reading>Shea</reading>, who hisses <reading>し</reading> through her teeth every time the till beeps too loud. The clerk never breaks his salute, but Shea flinches at every beep, still hissing it under her breath at closing.

k-descend.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 降 as a steep staircase cut into a mountainside, above a distant <radical>village</radical> at the bottom, two hurried <radical>trailing foot</radical>prints stamped down the steps. A crate tips off the vending machine and thunders down every step, bottles bouncing all the way down. A hill with feet already halfway down it: <kanji>descend</kanji>.
k-descend.reading_mnemonic: Koichi treks up that same trail himself to restock the vending machine. When the last case slips from his arms and crashes down every step behind him, he just sighs 「<reading>こう</reading>」 — more <reading>cough</reading> than word — and watches it disappear downhill.

k-transit.meaning_mnemonic: See 渡 as <radical>water</radical> drawn in three dripping strokes beside a row of measured footprints, like someone counting each step with a raised <radical>right hand</radical> from one bank to a <radical>shelter</radical> on the far side. The current never covers the marks. That is <kanji>transit</kanji>: crossing counted out, step by step.
k-transit.reading_mnemonic: Toto wades into the shallows with a sample door strapped to his shell, testing each stepping stone before he trusts it. Every plant of his foot lands with a flat 「<reading>と</reading>」, like a knuckle rapping a <reading>door</reading>, all the way to the far bank.

k-dwell.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 住 as one tall lamp, its <radical>jewel</radical>-capped finial catching light, beside a smaller post — planted by some <radical>person</radical> in the same square of ground for years. Moss climbs both at the same slow rate, each <radical>drop</radical> of dew feeding it. Planted in one place so long it has stopped being separate from it: <kanji>dwell</kanji>.
k-dwell.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat never wanders past the mossy steps — Jusuke, who has lived under the bell so long nobody remembers him arriving. Every time it tolls, he grumbles <reading>じゅう</reading>, low in his throat, like the word <reading>chew</reading> dragged out twice as long.

k-nothingness.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 無 as a school gym floor scorched flat by a stage fire the night before a show. Every prop is gone, only faint threads of smoke rising off the ash line where the curtain stood. Walk onto that floor: <radical>nothingness</radical> left to trip on, nothing to see, just an empty rectangle. <kanji>None</kanji> of it remains.
k-nothingness.reading_mnemonic: A stray cow named Muu wanders into that same burned-out gym through Sei's echoing hallway, nobody around to shoo her out. Her only sound bounces off the bare walls, a flat <reading>む</reading>, like a drawn-out <reading>moo</reading> nobody is there to hear.

k-first-time.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you grab the frayed rope and swing the huge bell for the <radical>first time</radical> in your life. The clapper catches wrong, and instead of a clean toll it screeches like a rusty gate, sending every cat bolting off at once. k-first-time.reading_mnemonic: Still ringing in your ears, the shrine's fattest cat gives one hoarse, botched yowl — not a full meow, just a wheezy <reading>しょ</reading>, like a magician trying to <reading>show</reading> off a trick that didn't land. Every disastrous first attempt at that bell gets remembered by that one broken sound.

k-department.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school has one door of <radical>grain</radical>-wood at the end of the main hallway, a <radical>dipper</radical> hanging by it to tally who passes through. Its plaque is nailed on crooked, at an angle no carpenter would allow. Every subject in the building funnels through that single lopsided doorway: the <kanji>department</kanji>.
k-department.reading_mnemonic: Kaa perches on the power line above that crooked doorway and coughs a puny puff of flame that singes the plaque a shade darker each week. The cough comes out hoarse and flat, <reading>か</reading>, like a stalling <reading>car</reading> engine — the sound the school now associates with that overworked door.

k-utmost.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, under the beating <radical>sun</radical>, past where the vending machine has any business being, <radical>one</radical> hiker drops face-first onto the last flat rock. His <radical>right hand</radical> scrapes for a grip as his <radical>ear</radical>s ring. There's no path beyond it — just the edge of what the trail can give: the <kanji>utmost</kanji>.

k-topic.meaning_mnemonic: Above the school gate, someone has bolted one steel <radical>page</radical> of a plaque so heavy it will never come down, catching the <radical>sun</radical> each morning. He throws his head back and wails his own name, <reading>Dai</reading>, at a pitch that registers as <reading>だい</reading> on every seismograph in town, and the plaque shudders on its bolts.

k-promise.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, two friends <radical>wrap</radical> a rope of braided <radical>thread</radical> around two posts and swear to meet on this exact spot every year — a promise sealed with a knot. k-promise.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Yaku</reading> checks that knot every morning, tugging it once and grunting 「<reading>やく</reading>」 in satisfaction when it holds. He does the same next year when it has shrunk another inch — the promise, apparently, unbroken.

k-sound.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the steep mountain trail, the one improbable vending machine finally takes your coin. It drops a can with a clang so loud it bounces off every rock on the way down. That clang, ringing back at you from every side at once, is the only <radical>sound</radical> for miles — pure <kanji>noise</kanji>, echoing on and on.
k-sound.reading_mnemonic: Every clang like that wakes something on the mountain: an echo spirit called <reading>On</reading>, who repeats the vending machine's ring straight back at you, moaning <reading>おん</reading> in the exact pitch of the can hitting the tray, over and over until the trail goes quiet.

k-whole.meaning_mnemonic: At closing time, Koichi, one <radical>person</radical> behind the till, stops itemizing the shelf. k-medicine.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the back shelf holds bottles kept <radical>ice</radical>-cold, <radical>grass</radical> and <radical>tree</radical> leaves poking from every cap, dripping bitter syrup onto the tiles. That crooked, leafy shelf is exactly how the character is drawn: <kanji>medicine</kanji>.
k-medicine.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>Yak</reading> shoulders through the konbini door, snuffles the dripping medicine shelf, and swallows a whole bottle in one gulp. Its stomach gurgles, it throws its huge head back, and out comes a groaning <reading>やく</reading> loud enough to rattle the onigiri shelf.

k-revolve.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a single cart wheel off a <radical>vehicle</radical>, drawn mid-spin. It doesn't stop at the bend: it whips around <radical>two</radical> full turns, coiling tight as a <radical>cocoon</radical>, and keeps going in one dizzy loop downhill: <kanji>revolve</kanji>.
k-revolve.reading_mnemonic: At the bottom of the trail the loose wheel clips the vending machine, and one stray coin spins out and won't lie flat, circling the gravel — a lone <reading>ten</reading>-yen piece. The hiker chases it, muttering <reading>てん</reading> each time it wobbles past again.

k-fall.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a stone letting go of the <radical>grass</radical>y riverbank edge. k-fall.reading_mnemonic: Downstream, the fisherman who missed the splash finds the culprit lodged in the shallows: a plain grey <reading>rock</reading>. He nudges it loose with his boot, and it thunks back under the surface with a flat, hollow <reading>らく</reading>.

k-beforehand.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning before the shutters lift, a <radical>hook</radical> with a sharp <radical>barb</radical> drops from the ceiling and snags tomorrow's delivery truck through <radical>one</radical> hole in time, hauling in rice balls that haven't been made yet. k-beforehand.reading_mnemonic: The hook-wielder greeter, a lanky clerk everyone calls <reading>Yo</reading>, hollers 「<reading>よ</reading>」 every time a snagged delivery drops through the hole in time. One flat syllable for every rice ball a day too soon.

k-grade.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the trail, a stonemason has chiseled the cliff into a staircase for decades, guarding it with a <radical>pike</radical>. He refuses anyone past the third stair. k-grade.reading_mnemonic: The stonemason, a squat old man everyone on the trail calls <reading>Dan</reading>, stamps your hiking permit. He grunts 「<reading>だん</reading>」 once for every stair he's decided you're worthy of, then turns his back.

k-nickname.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning on Sei's school field, a rooster on the fence handles roll call instead of the teacher, its <radical>mouth</radical> wrapped in a feathery <radical>wrap</radical>. It refuses to crow anyone's number. <radical>One</radical> by one, it screeches the nickname class gave you last week, until the field rings with everyone's most embarrassing <kanji>nickname</kanji>.
k-nickname.reading_mnemonic: The rooster itself has a name — the groundskeeper calls it <reading>Go</reading>. Every crow comes out as one long 「<reading>ごう</reading>」, stretched over the whole field, until the flag finally goes up and class begins.

k-plank.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a single wide plank of <radical>tree</radical>-wood has lain half in the water and half in the mud, propped against a low <radical>cliff</radical> for as long as anyone remembers. It splits down the center with every storm, but villagers' <radical>right hand</radical>s keep dragging it back to lay flat: the only board wide enough to cross on, a <kanji>plank</kanji>.
k-plank.reading_mnemonic: Downstream at the same crossing, the chef <reading>Han</reading> — the one who serves every dish split exactly in half — squats over the cracked plank and slices his lunch on it. He mutters 「<reading>はん</reading>」 with each cut: half for him, half for the current.

k-storey.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a tall staircase carved into the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, overlooking a <radical>village</radical> below. Each step, a little <radical>white</radical>r and greener than the last, climbs past the enormous bell toward a floor you can't yet see. <radical>Compare</radical> any two steps and one always sits higher: a <kanji>storey</kanji>.
k-storey.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>Kai</reading> climbs the shrine steps every morning, counting each landing aloud so he doesn't lose track: <reading>かい</reading>, one floor, <reading>かい</reading>, another. The cats sunning themselves on the steps stop washing just to watch him pass.
k-storey.description: 階 rarely stands alone as the everyday word for a storey. In practice it almost always attaches to a number as the counter for building floors. きざはし is a rare, literary reading for a staircase; かい is the reading actually used day to day.

k-craft.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 工 as a squat steel I-beam — flat cap on top, flat foot on the bottom, one spine welded straight down the middle: pure <radical>construction</radical>. A crew winches it upright on a bare lot and bolts it in before a single wall exists. That lone beam is the first thing raised on any job site: the shape of <kanji>craft</kanji> itself.
k-craft.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wheels his restocking cart past the freshly bolted beam and clips his elbow on the corner. He lets out a flat <reading>coo</reading>, dragging the vowel out long like his till's slow beep: <reading>こう</reading>. Then he reroutes the onigiri delivery around it.

k-spot.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 点 as a hanko, carved like a tiny <radical>divination</radical> stick, stamped too hard through the school's front <radical>mouth</radical>way onto a test paper. The seal bursts, ink scattering like sparks off <radical>fire</radical>. Four droplets spatter across the score box, each drying into its own dark, unmistakable <kanji>spot</kanji>.
k-spot.reading_mnemonic: The hall monitor everyone just calls <reading>Ten</reading> finds the spattered test on the floor. He holds up all ten fingers, hissing 「<reading>てん</reading>」, counting the ink spots one by one before confiscating the paper.

k-meadow.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 原 as a <radical>small</radical> slab of <radical>white</radical> rock jutting low over a <radical>cliff</radical> above the mountain trail. A thin spring bleeds out from underneath, spreading downhill until the ground opens into a flat <kanji>meadow</kanji> of undisturbed grass. This is where the trail's only water starts.
k-meadow.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named <reading>Gen</reading> kneels at the spring to refill her bottle, and the cold hits her wrist so hard she yelps <reading>げん</reading>, sharp enough that the grasshoppers in the meadow scatter for cover.

k-lady.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 婦 as a <radical>woman</radical> named Fumi, sweeping Grandma Kane's shrine steps at dawn under the <radical>cover</radical> of a long apron of <radical>cloth</radical>. Her <radical>broom</radical> scrapes stone in the same rhythm every morning while the shrine cats scatter. She works top to bottom without looking up: the picture of a <kanji>lady</kanji> running her own household.
k-lady.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, Fumi leans her broom against the rail and blows out a long <reading>phew</reading> — a breathy 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 that scatters the incense smoke. Then she picks the broom up to finish the steps.

k-idea.meaning_mnemonic: In a hallway at Sei's school, picture the kanji as one image: a heavy iron lid clamped over a beating <radical>heart</radical>, muffling every <radical>sound</radical> of its thump. Pressure builds until the lid cracks a finger's width. A single bright spark hisses free through the gap: that spark, still hot, is the <kanji>idea</kanji>.
k-idea.reading_mnemonic: That escaped spark turns out to be Eeko, a firefly who only ever says one sound. She loops once around the lockers and lets out a bright <reading>い</reading> — an <reading>eek</reading>-thin squeak of light — before ducking back through the crack in the lid to cool off.

k-change.meaning_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini, a customer catches his own reflection in the till's dark screen. On the left he stands upright, a normal <radical>person</radical>; on the right that body has folded double and sprouted a stubby tail. One shape slides into the other, mid-blink: <kanji>change</kanji>.
k-change.reading_mnemonic: Outside the window, Kaa the fire-breathing crow has been watching the whole trick from the power line. He can't hold it in — he lets out a hoarse <reading>か</reading>, the same rasp as his name, <reading>Kaa</reading>, and a puff of flame scorches the wire above the sliding doors.

k-sentence.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cat sleeps spread-eagle across the mossy steps, arms flung wide, legs crossed at the ankle. Afternoon light slats through the eaves. It lands across her fur in neat, deliberate lines of <radical>writing</radical>, until her whole back reads as one finished <kanji>sentence</kanji>.
k-sentence.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the rabbit twins, lean over the cat arguing about how it ends. One twin insists it needs a flourish on top, like a bread <reading>bun</reading>, and keeps hollering <reading>ぶん</reading> until the enormous bell rings and the cat twitches the whole sentence into a blur.

k-method.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the <radical>water</radical> doesn't get to wander. Picture the whole kanji as a stone flume packed with <radical>earth</radical>, its narrow mouth sealed like a <radical>cocoon</radical>, forcing every drop through one channel, same order, no shortcuts. That fixed channel, followed exactly, is the <kanji>method</kanji>.
k-method.reading_mnemonic: Hou, an owl who lives on the flume post, keeps watch for cheaters. Whenever a drop tries to leap the channel early, he swivels his head and hoots <reading>ほう</reading> — a low <reading>whoa</reading> that echoes off the water — until the drop falls back into line.

k-generation.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, three fence posts lean out of the moss at different heights. A groundskeeper strings one rope low for the toddlers, higher for the parents, higher still for the grandparents, refusing to leave until all three cross the same posts. The tangle reads as one <radical>generation</radical> roped to the next: a whole <kanji>society</kanji>.
k-generation.reading_mnemonic: Sei, hand up before anyone asks, elbows in to fix the groundskeeper's ropes and gets both ankles lassoed for it. She yanks free, smooths her uniform, and announces the fix in one clipped syllable that sounds exactly like you'd <reading>say</reading> it: <reading>せい</reading>.

k-world.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the vending machine, the ground drops away and the valley opens below: a <radical>rice field</radical> after rice field, boxed by its own low fence. A lone <radical>person</radical> stands on two <radical>human legs</radical> at the edge, taking it all in — every field at once, hemmed edge to edge, boundaries adding up to the whole <kanji>world</kanji>.
k-world.reading_mnemonic: The hiker who dragged you up here — you call him <reading>Kai</reading> for the noise he makes at every switchback — doubles over at the summit. He lets out one long 「<reading>かい</reading>」 of relief before he looks at the view.

k-politics.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field, the flagpole with its <radical>chevron</radical> pennant has bent sideways overnight. Sei drags it upright and raps it with a <radical>tap</radical> of her pointer each time it starts to <radical>stop</radical> and slump. The whole field stands at attention around one stick beaten straight. That correcting by force is <kanji>politics</kanji>: government as the art of straightening what keeps slumping.
k-politics.reading_mnemonic: Sei doesn't stop at the flagpole. She marches the whole class into rows and claps them straight. Every clap lands on the same syllable, sharp as a ruler on a desk: 「<reading>せい</reading>」 — the way you'd <reading>say</reading> a drill sergeant's count.

k-reign.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the <radical>water</radical> thrashes every direction, slapping washing out of people's hands. Someone stacks stones into a low wall with a narrow <radical>mouth</radical> gap, sealed tight as a <radical>cocoon</radical>, and the water that fought all morning collects behind it into one flat, silent pool. That taming of the flood is <kanji>reign</kanji>: to calm down.
k-reign.reading_mnemonic: The stone-stacker, a quiet type the other kids call <reading>Ji</reading> because he never says more than one syllable, watches his pool go still and finally speaks: <reading>じ</reading>, and nothing else, satisfied.

k-sex.meaning_mnemonic: 性 shows up as one stamped box on a school health form: the box for your inborn nature, straight from the <radical>heart</radical> of your <radical>life</radical>. Sei isn't satisfied checking it once — he stamps it three times and asks the nurse to grade his nature like an exam. Stamped and graded: that is your <kanji>sex</kanji>, your gender, your nature.
k-sex.reading_mnemonic: The nurse, exhausted, waves the form away and tells him to just <reading>say</reading> his name and leave — Sei straightens up and corrects her anyway: it's <reading>せい</reading>, properly stamped, thank you.

k-inter.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the water sits mirror-still beside a lone <radical>tree</radical>: a hiker leans over and his reflection leans back, matching every twitch of his <radical>eye</radical>. He waves, the water waves back; he frowns, it frowns back — two sides doing the same thing to each other. That two-way mirroring is <kanji>inter-</kanji>: mutual, together.
k-inter.reading_mnemonic: The hiker, Sou, leans in close and mutters 「<reading>そう</reading>」 to his own reflection, daring it to answer. Right on cue, impossibly, the water mutters <reading>so</reading> straight back at him — word for word, syllable for syllable.

k-guest.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine atop the trail sits under its little <radical>roof</radical>, the only comfort after that steep climb. A hiker treats it like a hotel lobby: he drops his pack, kicks off his boots, <radical>trailing foot</radical>prints in the gravel. He opens his <radical>mouth</radical>, waiting for someone to bring him tea, self-appointed as the honored <kanji>guest</kanji>.
k-guest.reading_mnemonic: His ride up was a foul-tempered <reading>yak</reading> that refuses to leave the summit, planting itself by the machine like it's checked into a hotel. A guide radios down that a 「<reading>きゃく</reading>」 has arrived and shows no sign of ever checking out.

k-public.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi never locks the konbini doors — day, night, holiday, no difference — because in his head the shop stopped being his years ago and became everyone's. He restocks the onigiri shelf for total strangers like a prince tending his domain, open to anyone who walks in. That is 公: public, official, everyone's business.
k-public.reading_mnemonic: Regulars don't bother with his whole name anymore — they just call out the long stretched <reading>Ko</reading> of 'Koichi' as he blurs past restocking, and it comes out as one clipped <reading>こう</reading>, because efficiency belongs to the public queue, not to small talk.

k-profit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 利 as one tool: a thin blade lying flat beside a heavy stalk of grain, both leaning the same way, like a scale about to tip. At Koichi's konbini the clerk nicks a rice sack's string with that blade, and the sack weighs heavier after the cut than before. The register just prints profit.
k-profit.reading_mnemonic: At the same konbini scale, the clerk keeps a dry <reading>reed</reading> tucked behind his ear for luck, and every time a sack outweighs itself he snaps the reed and grins, muttering a stretched <reading>り</reading> like he just got away with something.

k-task.meaning_mnemonic: See 務 as one overloaded figure: a spear on one shoulder, a stick raised in a striking hand, and one arm flexed hard under the weight — three demands crammed onto a single body, none optional. On the mountain trail the guide carries all three past every switchback, only dropping his shoulders at the vending machine on top. The task is done.
k-task.reading_mnemonic: A cow that wandered up years ago still blocks the trail near that vending machine until every task is read aloud to her. She answers each one with a flat <reading>moo</reading>, and that same flat sound is the reading <reading>む</reading> — one syllable, no complaints, task acknowledged.

k-transport.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 輸 as one vehicle: a wagon's two wheels bolted onto a hollowed dugout boat's hull, rolling the riverbank path and floating once the bank drops away. Crates get loaded on and it shoves off — wheels spinning uselessly underwater, hull scraping stone on land — yet the ugly thing drags everything across. That is transport.
k-transport.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman poling this contraption never learns anyone's name, so he calls every passenger the same drawn-out word as the wheels hit water: a long <reading>you</reading>. That same stretched syllable is the reading <reading>ゆ</reading>, hollered once as the crates lurch forward and the hull scrapes off from the bank.

k-status.meaning_mnemonic: See 格 as one gnarled tree at Grandma Kane's shrine, where each branch forks off at its own height and stops there, holding exactly one cat and no other — the top branch for the biggest cat, the lowest for the newest arrival. No cat may sit on a branch that isn't hers. That fixed, branch-by-branch order is status.
k-status.reading_mnemonic: Every visitor who climbs the shrine's mossy steps and sees the cats ranked branch by branch just stops and <reading>gawks</reading>, throat catching on the same flat sound as the reading <reading>かく</reading>. The shrine's one enormous bell seems to echo it back once for every branch in the tree.

k-gate.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two matching wooden panels, hinged and identical, standing across from each other at Grandma Kane's shrine, flanking the mossy steps. A cat darts between them and both panels swing shut at once, clapping together with a boom that sets the enormous bell ringing. Twin doors that only work as a pair — that's a gate.
k-gate.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, argue at Grandma Kane's shrine, each ending every sentence with a flat <reading>もん</reading> — book-nerd slang for obviously. They stand together like the gate's own twin panels, and every <reading>Mon</reading> makes the enormous bell shiver on its hook.

k-turn-into.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one battered vending machine waits by the summit sign. A hiker feeds it a coin, and instead of a drink, the whole machine shudders, its panels folding and reforming until it isn't a vending machine anymore — it's a wooden bench, still warm. That's turn into: one thing reshaping into another.
k-turn-into.reading_mnemonic: Sei reaches the summit first, hand up before anyone can ask, and plants herself by the vending machine that just turned into a bench. She declares it like a quiz answer: a crisp, smug <reading>せい</reading>, and hikers who arrive late swear they can still hear that <reading>say</reading> echo off the rocks.

k-sort-of.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer holds up an onigiri with the label torn clean off and asks what's inside. The clerk squints at it, sniffs it once, then waves a hand vaguely at the whole shelf — sort of like those, probably that kind of thing. Nobody presses further; sort of thing turns out to be a real answer here.
k-sort-of.reading_mnemonic: The clerk, whom regulars just call <reading>Zen</reading> for his permanent shrug, mutters a flat <reading>ぜん</reading> every time someone asks for specifics, sliding the mystery onigiri back onto the shelf without another word. Say his name fast enough and it collapses into the same flat <reading>ぜん</reading> — shrug included.

k-mask.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, something pale and square drifts down with the current — a blank wooden mask, one oval outline, two carved eye-holes. Someone wades in, fishes it out, and holds it right over their own face. Their expression vanishes, replaced by the mask's flat stare. That's a mask — a face swapped for a face.
k-mask.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman who drags it from the water, everyone calls him <reading>Men</reading> for the grunt he gives instead of talking, holds the mask to the sky and lets out a low <reading>めん</reading> like a verdict. From then on, every mask pulled from that river gets the same flat <reading>めん</reading> before anyone's allowed to touch it.

k-demolition.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat leaps onto the bell rope just to swing on it. The rope snaps, the enormous bell tears free, and it thunders down the mossy steps, cracking three of them to rubble. Grandma Kane just sighs — another Tuesday of demolition.
k-demolition.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's apprentice, a boy named <reading>Kai</reading>, surveys the wreckage and sighs the count out loud: <reading>かい</reading> — the third bell disaster this year alone. He says it flat, already reaching for the broom.

k-bring-up.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, the groundskeeper plants one droopy sunflower seedling in an old milk carton and waters it every recess. By the third week it has shot up past the goalposts, leaves like small hands reaching for the sky — proof of raising something up.
k-bring-up.reading_mnemonic: A tiny kid named <reading>Iku</reading> waters the sunflower every morning before the bell, chanting <reading>いく</reading>, いく, grow already — as if the word itself could drag the stalk taller.

k-drought.meaning_mnemonic: The riverbank that should be rushing with water is nothing but a maze of cracked, sun-baked mud plates. A heron stands in the middle on one leg, unable to remember what wet ground even felt like — the whole bank has gone bone dry, a total drought.
k-drought.reading_mnemonic: The same heron kicks an empty tin <reading>can</reading> across the cracked mud out of pure boredom. It rolls to a stop with a hollow <reading>かん</reading> — the only sound this drought-cracked riverbank makes all summer.

k-get-wet.meaning_mnemonic: A customer bursts through the door of Koichi's konbini soaked from collar to shoe, rain sheeting off him in one long trail across the tile straight to the onigiri shelf. He leaves a puddle so deep the beeping till stutters and dies — everything about him has gotten wet.
k-get-wet.reading_mnemonic: Koichi mops the puddle and mutters <reading>じゅ</reading>, じゅ, like he's wringing the sound out of a sponge — it comes out exactly like the first syllable of <reading>juice</reading>, which is unfortunately also what the floor now smells like.
k-get-wet.description: This character mostly means plain physical wetness — rain, tears, sweat. The "make love" sense is idiomatic, from a fixed phrase for an intimate scene in film or drama. On its own as a verb, it almost always just means damp, not romance.

k-correct.meaning_mnemonic: On the school sports field, the coach chalks one line across the track and rules that only a toe planted exactly on it counts. Every runner skids past it or stops short — except Sei, uniform still spotless, who lands a toe dead on the line without even trying, smug before the whistle even blows: correct.
k-correct.reading_mnemonic: Back in the classroom, the teacher asks who stopped exactly on the line. Sei's hand shoots up before she finishes asking, and he answers with his own name like it settles it: <reading>Sei</reading>, <reading>せい</reading> — crisp, correct, a little too pleased with himself.

k-straightaway.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, everything bends — the reeds, the ripples, the rope holding the ferry to its post. Only the ferryman's eye stays fixed dead ahead on the far bank. He refuses to glance down at the crooked water and poles straightaway across, blunt and honest about exactly where he's going: straight, no detour.
k-straightaway.reading_mnemonic: On the far bank, kids call the ferryman Chalky, because his pole is an actual stick of chalk that drags one straight white line across the water on every crossing. Ask him why and he barks the same flat answer every time: <reading>ちょく</reading>, <reading>chalk</reading> — straight, immediate, no explanation given.

k-suffering.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs the last onigiri off the shelf by the door and bites in before checking the date. It's turned — bitter, warm, wrong — and his whole face folds in on itself right there under the fluorescent lights, the till beeping behind him like it's keeping score of his suffering.
k-suffering.reading_mnemonic: He doesn't groan, exactly — what comes out is a strangled little <reading>coo</reading>, like a dove that swallowed a coin. The cashier doesn't even look up. She's heard that same <reading>く</reading> from every unlucky customer who trusted that shelf after dark.

k-even.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail climbs brutal and uneven for an hour, every step steeper than the last, until it just stops — the ground opens into one perfectly flat clearing around the vending machine at the top, level in every direction, not a single rock out of place. After all that chaos, it's suddenly, completely even.
k-even.reading_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself into the clearing, drops his pack, and lets out one long <reading>hey</reading> — half greeting to the vending machine, half sigh at finally standing on ground that doesn't fight back. That flat exhale is exactly the sound of <reading>へい</reading>: level, calm, done.

k-clear-up.meaning_mnemonic: Rain floods the school's sports field mid-relay, runners skidding through mud while the crowd groans under dripping umbrellas. Then the clouds simply tear apart overhead, one shaft of sun lands square on the finish line, steam lifts off the soaked track, and the whole field is suddenly, brightly clear up.
k-clear-up.reading_mnemonic: As the sky clears, Sei's hand shoots up first as always, uniform spotless despite the mud, and she announces it to the whole field, loud and smug: <reading>せい</reading> — like she's the one who <reading>said</reading> the sky would clear.

k-heat.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the microwave runs three full cycles on one forgotten onigiri, the wrapper bubbling and warping, the till beeping in panic behind the counter. When the door finally pops open, a wall of heat rolls out thick enough to fog the whole drink case. Heat, plain and total.
k-heat.reading_mnemonic: The clerk mopping her forehead at the register is nicknamed <reading>Netsu</reading> for it, and every time that wall of heat rolls out she groans the sound of her own name, <reading>ねつ</reading>, dragging it out like she's wading through hot fishing nets.

k-negative.meaning_mnemonic: A stiff figure plants itself at the top of Grandma Kane's mossy steps, arms flung straight out, ankles crossed tight, blocking the path to the enormous bell. Cats stream around its legs but it will not move, will not ring, will not budge — every request meets the same flat refusal. Negative.
k-negative.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat everyone calls <reading>Fu</reading>, curled against the stubborn figure's crossed feet, doesn't hiss so much as sigh through her nose — a flat little <reading>ふ</reading> of a breath, unimpressed by every visitor who tries to squeeze past.
k-negative.description: This kanji almost never stands alone in real sentences; you meet it glued to the front of other words as a flat negation prefix, closer to un- or non- in English than a standalone word for bad.

k-precipitous.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail narrows to a knife-edge ridge, the path pinching to nothing between two sheer drops, one wrong step from the vending machine improbably waiting at the top. No one has ever reached it and no one ever will — the position is precipitous, impregnable, sealed off from the world.
k-precipitous.reading_mnemonic: Guarding that narrow ledge is <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who never leaves his wall of antique swords, and every hiker who eyes the vending machine past him gets one warning bark of <reading>けん</reading> before he bares a blade in his teeth.
k-precipitous.description: Beyond the literal steep-cliff picture, this kanji usually carries a broader sense of danger or risk in real vocabulary — insurance, adventure, hazard — rather than physical steepness itself.

k-seethe.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the hot water tap for cup noodles sticks wide open. The broth climbs past the rim in fat white bubbles, hissing and multiplying until foam rolls off the counter and drips past the onigiri shelf. The clerk just watches it seethe, boil, and go faintly sour under the fluorescent lights.
k-seethe.reading_mnemonic: A jumpy regular named <reading>Futz</reading> keeps mashing the button, muttering <reading>ふつ</reading>, ふつ under his breath every time the noodle water surges past the rim. Say his nervous little ふつ ふつ and the reading is stuck in your head with the foam.

k-burn.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a cat leaps onto the offering shelf and topples a candle into a bundle of incense sticks. They catch one by one, each tip glowing orange, until the whole bundle flares into a blaze crackling under the enormous bell before anyone notices the smoke.
k-burn.reading_mnemonic: The neighborhood kids call Grandma Kane <reading>Nan</reading>, and when the incense flares she comes flying out stamping sparks off the mossy steps, yelling the cat's name so fast it comes out <reading>ねん</reading>. Picture Nan hollering ねん at that cat, and the reading burns itself in.

k-current.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a sandal slips off the washing stones and the current takes it instantly, spinning it past the reeds and around the bend before anyone can wade in. Nothing dropped here stays put; the whole river is one long current pulling everything the same direction, gone before you can call after it.
k-current.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Ryu</reading> wades out too far and the current takes him too, his voice trailing off in a long <reading>りゅう</reading>, りゅう as he's carried past the reeds and around the bend, already too far off to reach. Say Ryu's fading りゅう and you have the reading.

k-times.meaning_mnemonic: From above, Sei's running track looks like one square course boxed inside a bigger square fence, the same loop traced again and again by whoever's running it. Each full lap around that boxed-in course is one more time, and the count just keeps climbing while the loop never changes shape.
k-times.reading_mnemonic: Sei's PE teacher, a man everyone calls <reading>Kai</reading>, stands at the gate barking a number each time a runner completes the loop: <reading>かい</reading>, かい, かい, one shout per lap. By the tenth lap nobody's counting anything but Kai's voice landing on かい.

k-surpass.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail switches back for an hour, calves burning, every ridge a good place to quit. Then a vending machine appears, glowing at the very top, absurdly out of place. You ignore every sane stopping point and just keep going, legs shaking, until you surpass the last ridge and reach it.
k-surpass.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, a hiker named <reading>Etsu</reading> collapses against the vending machine and groans <reading>えつ</reading> between gasps — the same groan echoes down the trail every time someone else finally surpasses that last ridge.

k-traffic.meaning_mnemonic: The bell rings and the school hallway turns into a river of students, shoulders knocking, bags swinging, a current with nowhere to stop. Nobody walks — they get carried by the crush from one end of the echoing hallway to the other, an unbroken flow of traffic passing straight through, like the whole building is one long avenue.
k-traffic.reading_mnemonic: A hall monitor named <reading>Tsuu</reading> stands in the doorway blowing one note — <reading>つう</reading> — every few seconds, waving the flood of students through without ever telling them to stop. By the fortieth <reading>つう</reading> you can still hear it at home.

k-severance.meaning_mnemonic: You're halfway across the rope bridge at the riverbank when a strand snaps with a crack, and the whole bridge swings shut behind you like a door slamming. There's no going back — the path behind you has been cut clean through, severed, and the only choice left is to refuse turning around.
k-severance.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Dan</reading> stands at the riverbank when his line goes slack, and he shouts <reading>だん</reading> — the exact sound of a taut line snapping in half, sharp and final, the same clean break that just cut the bridge in two behind you.

k-help.meaning_mnemonic: A customer at Koichi's konbini drops an armful of onigiri and folds straight toward the fluorescent-bright floor. Koichi vaults the counter, catches them under the arms, and hauls them back onto their feet before the till even finishes beeping — pure help, the instinct to rescue someone before you've decided to.
k-help.reading_mnemonic: Back on their feet, the rescued customer, who Koichi has started calling <reading>Jo</reading>, breathes out a long shaky <reading>じょ</reading>, half relief and half embarrassment, still clutching the onigiri that never hit the floor.

k-stubborn.meaning_mnemonic: 頑 is a boulder squatting dead center of the mountain trail, a face gouged into the granite by decades of wind — jaw set, eyes narrowed. Hikers heave against it, bribe it with vending-machine snacks, beg. It doesn't roll an inch. That immovable, deliberate refusal is the whole meaning: stubborn.
k-stubborn.reading_mnemonic: Every time a hiker shoves the boulder, a hermit camped beside it cups his hands and grunts <reading>がん</reading> — the same flat sound, like someone saying <reading>gone</reading> through a clenched jaw. It's the only word he says. The boulder still hasn't moved.

k-accustomed.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the konbini clerk at 3am, scanning onigiri without ever glancing down — barcode beep, bag, next, beep, bag, next — his hands moving faster than his half-asleep eyes. Ten thousand nights of the same shift ground the motion into muscle memory. He's not thinking about it anymore. He's simply accustomed to it.
k-accustomed.reading_mnemonic: Behind the counter, Koichi restocks the drink case so many times his hand does it alone — each can lands with a flat clink that sounds like <reading>かん</reading>, someone saying <reading>khan</reading> without the h. He's stopped hearing it. That's how accustomed he's become.

k-overdo.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the riverbank at flood stage: the water hits the marker post, and then keeps going — past it, past the next post, past the path, still climbing. It doesn't know how to stop at the line. That refusal to quit at the edge, going further than needed, is overdoing it — exceeding, going beyond.
k-overdo.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow watches from the power line above the flooded bank. One puff of flame would do, but she can't stop — she keeps cawing <reading>か</reading>, <reading>か</reading>, like someone stuck repeating <reading>kah</reading>, torching the same branch long after it's ash.
